title: Your chats on every device — follow-ups after checking the code

steps.headline: The design is for every user's devices. Yours are only the test case.
steps.changed: Stated, not asked: the first deck was written around your laptop, desktop and phone. The design itself is written for any mix of Windows, Mac, Linux and Android devices a user owns.
steps.notice: Nothing in the app will name or assume specific machines; every rule works for one device or ten.

steps.path: Any chat, on any of your devices
steps.headline: One device hosts a chat. Every other device shows it live and types into it, identical except for a chip naming the host.
steps.changed: Stated from your answers: a chat always runs on one device, its host. Other devices are windows onto it, word by word, with no separate copy to collide.
steps.notice: You stop noticing which device is doing the work. The chip is the only tell, and tapping it is the only way to move a chat while its host is online.

steps.path: A chat whose host went offline
steps.headline: A host changes only when you tap the chip, or when the host is offline and you tap Continue here. The half-finished reply is dropped.
steps.changed: Stated from your answers: no automatic moves, no surprise switches, and the notice spells out what the new device may lack before you continue.
steps.notice: A chat whose host is away sits readable with a notice until you decide. Nothing happens behind your back.

steps.path: The current handoff and takeover code
steps.headline: The current handoff and takeover system is replaced, not patched. No fixes to it ship before the new design is agreed.
steps.changed: Stated from your answer on phasing: the roughly 1,600 lines that do today's 25-second handoff, takeover dialogs and moved-gate are retired by the new design rather than improved first.
steps.notice: Today's warnings and occasional lost messages stay as they are until the new system lands. The two lost Nov 5 exchanges stay in their conflict copies, per your No.

steps.intro: Live word-by-word viewing needs a connection between two devices at that moment. Today the only such link is Tailscale, which most users will never install.

steps.path: Backup & Sync and Remote access in settings
steps.headline: How should a user's devices connect for live viewing?
steps.today: A phone can watch a computer only over Tailscale, a separate app the user installs and signs into on every device. Home wifi is refused on purpose since the Oct 30 security review. The sync service already gives every signed-in account a private online room, but it carries only tiny notices.
steps.problem: Asking every user to install Tailscale rules out most of them. Any other path is new work and has its own cost.
steps.proposal: Pick every path the app should support. The recommended one is the path that works for everyone with no setup.

options.label: Through YouCoded's own service
pros: Works from anywhere with nothing to install; signing in to the app is the only setup.
The account room, sign-in and device identities already exist; the relay part is new.
cons: Every live word passes through a server you pay for, so cost grows with users.
Needs the next question's answer on encryption.

options.label: Direct, with the service as introducer
pros: Devices talk to each other directly after the service introduces them, so the server carries almost nothing.
cons: Direct connections fail behind many home routers and phone networks, so a relay is still needed as a fallback; the most complex option to build.

options.label: Tailscale
pros: Already works for the phone today; private, no server of yours involved.
cons: Users must install and sign in to a second app on every device; computer-to-computer viewing is still new work.

options.label: Same home wifi, directly
pros: Fast and free when both devices are at home.
cons: Reverses the Oct 30 decision unless the link is encrypted first; useless away from home.

steps.path: Anything that passes through YouCoded's service
steps.headline: If live chat text passes through YouCoded's service, may the service be able to read it?
steps.today: Sync already stores conversations in the user's own private GitHub space, which GitHub can read. The sync service itself sees only notices, never chat text.
steps.problem: A relay that can read chats is simpler to build and lets you debug it. One that cannot read them protects users from you, from a breach, and from legal requests, but if a user loses every device their key is gone with it.
steps.proposal: Pick what the service may see.

options.label: Service cannot read chats
pros: Matches the Oct 30 intent: conversations never travel readable.
A breach of the service exposes no chat text.
cons: Key management is new work: a key per account, handed to each new device at sign-in.
Lose every device and the live link's key is gone; the GitHub backup still restores the chats themselves.

options.label: Encrypted in transit only
pros: Simpler and quicker to build; easier to debug.
cons: Your server could read every live chat; users must trust you not to.

steps.headline: Who pays for the relay traffic?
steps.today: Sync is free because the user's own GitHub stores the files. The sync service's small notices cost you almost nothing.
steps.problem: Relaying live chats costs real money per active user per hour. A card already parks the idea of a paid tier for cloud sync.
steps.proposal: Pick how the cost is covered.

options.label: Free, with usage watched
pros: Nothing in the way of users; you see the real cost before deciding anything.
cons: You pay for everyone until you change course.

options.label: Part of a paid tier
pros: Covers its own cost from day one.
cons: Needs billing, which does not exist in the app; most users never see the feature.

options.label: Free up to a monthly limit
pros: Bounded cost.
cons: A chat that stops streaming mid-month is a confusing failure.

steps.intro: I inventoried everything a running chat holds beyond its messages. Most of it does not sync today, and some of it cannot.

steps.path: A chat continued on another device
steps.headline: How should a chat's surroundings move with it?
steps.today: Messages, titles and tags sync. A project folder under YouCoded Projects syncs as files to every device. Not synced: helper transcripts, undo history, memory notes, plans, saved tool output. Cannot move: running programs, open browser tabs, a half-answered permission prompt.
steps.problem: Your idea of a container per chat that moves between devices is one of three ways to get there, each with a different cost.
steps.proposal: Pick the mechanism to design around.

options.label: Host stays; sync the portable leftovers
pros: While the host is online nothing needs to move at all, which is your chosen model.
Helper transcripts, undo history, notes and plans are plain files; syncing them is modest work.
cons: Running programs and open browser tabs still die with an offline host; the Continue here notice says so.

options.label: A portable bundle per chat
pros: One package holds the chat, its files and history; move it and everything is there.
cons: Duplicates the project's files per chat, so disk use multiplies.
Still cannot carry running programs.

options.label: A real container per chat
pros: In principle the whole running environment, programs included, could pause on one device and resume on another.
cons: Not possible on Android or plain Windows; heavy on every platform; months of work before the first chat moves.

steps.path: A chat continued on another device
steps.headline: Which extra pieces must follow a chat to its new host?
steps.today: Only the main messages and the chat's title, tags and notes travel. Everything below stays on the device that made it.
steps.problem: Each piece is separate work and some are keyed to one machine's folder layout, so they need rewriting on the way.

options.label: Helper transcripts
pros: The assistant's side-workers' notes stay readable; a card already suspects their loss causes missed messages.
cons: None beyond size.

options.label: Undo history
pros: Undo an edit made on the other device.
cons: Keyed to the old device's exact folder paths, so it must be rewritten in transit; only meaningful for synced projects.

options.label: Memory notes and plans
pros: The assistant remembers the same things about a project everywhere.
cons: Keyed to a folder path today; needs a re-key.

options.label: Approved-permission rules
pros: Say yes to a tool once, on any device.
cons: Deliberately per machine today, because a phone and a work PC may deserve different trust.

options.label: Attached files and images
pros: A photo sent from the phone is there when the desktop hosts the chat.
cons: Live in temporary folders today; needs a permanent home per chat.

steps.path: A chat whose old host comes back
steps.headline: You continued a chat elsewhere after its host went offline. When the old host comes back, what happens to its leftover half-reply?
steps.today: Not possible today; the nearest thing is a conflict copy the app never shows.
steps.problem: The old host still holds the cut-off reply you chose to drop. Left alone it would re-sync as a second version of the chat, the exact split you said must never happen.
steps.proposal: Pick what the returning device does, automatically, the moment it sees the chat moved on without it.

options.label: Discard its leftover silently
pros: No split ever appears; the chat is identical everywhere again.
What it discards is only the reply you already chose to drop.
cons: If that reply had edited files on the old device, those edits remain there with no message explaining them.

options.label: Keep it as an archived fork
pros: Nothing is ever deleted; you can read what the old host had said.
cons: One archived entry per incident in the chat list, which is clutter for something you chose to drop.

options.label: Ask on the returning device
pros: You decide with the text in front of you.
cons: A dialog on a device you may not be looking at, about a reply you already dropped.

steps.intro: I checked what the phone can and cannot do today. It runs the same engine and the same sync as a computer, and it has synced project folders. Some tools are missing.

steps.path: Any chat hosted on the phone
steps.headline: The phone is missing some tools today. How should this design treat that gap?
steps.today: The phone runs Claude Code and native chats with files, search, background commands, hooks and the same sync as a computer. Missing: the assistant's browser, Office, admin commands, a folder picker and access to the phone's own photos and downloads, local models, and helper programs such as Python or npm.
steps.problem: Full parity is a project of its own. This design can assume it, wait for it, or work around it.

options.label: Assume parity; close gaps separately
pros: This design treats a phone exactly like a computer, as you want; the missing tools become their own work items and land in parallel.
cons: Until they land, a chat hosted on the phone may fail a step a computer would have done, and the assistant says so.

options.label: Close the gaps first
pros: The phone is a full host on day one.
cons: Delays every device feature by the time the phone work takes.

options.label: Phone views only until parity
pros: No half-working hosted chats on the phone.
cons: Contradicts your parity goal in the meantime; a phone with every computer off can only read.

steps.headline: Should every device hold every synced project, or only the ones it needs?
steps.today: Every device downloads every synced project in full, automatically, with no way to opt out. A phone with a 5 GB project downloads 5 GB.
steps.problem: Storage and data on a phone are scarce, yet hosting a project chat there needs the project's files present.
steps.proposal: Pick how projects spread across devices. You already chose list-then-open for chats; this is the same question for projects.

options.label: Download when a chat here needs it
pros: A phone stays small until you host a project chat on it; then the project arrives first and the chat starts.
cons: The first message to a project chat on a new device waits for the download, with a progress line.

options.label: You choose per device
pros: Full control: tick which projects each device holds.
cons: A chat for an unticked project cannot be hosted there until you change the setting.

options.label: Everything everywhere, as today
pros: Any device can host any chat instantly.
cons: Phones fill up; a big project blocks sync for a long time on first setup.

steps.path: A chat hosted on the phone with the screen off
steps.headline: How should the phone stay awake while it hosts a reply with the screen off?
steps.today: A background service keeps the engine running, but nothing holds the phone awake for a reply. Battery saving modes may pause it; this has never been measured. A 4-hour keep-awake exists only for remote access.
steps.problem: A reply paused mid-way looks like a vanished host to other devices. Holding the phone awake drains the battery.
steps.proposal: Pick the approach, knowing the first step is to measure what Android actually does.

options.label: Awake only while a reply runs
pros: Costs battery only during work; released the moment the reply ends, with a hard cap so it can never stick.
cons: Some phones ignore it in strict battery modes; the measurement will tell.

options.label: Ask to be exempt from battery saving
pros: The most reliable way to keep running.
cons: A scary system prompt at setup, and app stores frown on it without a clear reason.

options.label: Do nothing
pros: No battery cost.
cons: Replies hosted on the phone may stall whenever the screen turns off.

steps.intro: Three things the code research changed, and the two features you named: the chip and explicit forking.

steps.headline: Uploading before sleep: each system allows two to five seconds and a real upload takes far longer. What happens in that window?
steps.today: Closing the lid does nothing. An upload is a dozen steps and two trips to GitHub; sleep arrives first.
steps.problem: A full upload cannot fit. Holding the computer awake until it finishes is the stuck keep-awake you warned about.
steps.proposal: Pick what the sleeping device does with its few seconds.

options.label: Send a tiny note, upload on wake
pros: Fits easily: one short message to the service saying this device holds unsent messages for chat X.
Other devices show Laptop has newer messages instead of a stale chat; the real upload runs the moment it wakes.
cons: The messages themselves stay on the sleeping device until it wakes.

options.label: Try the full upload anyway
pros: Sometimes finishes on a fast connection.
cons: Usually cut off halfway; a half upload is worse to reason about than none.

options.label: Hold the device awake until uploaded
pros: The upload always completes.
cons: A hung upload keeps the laptop awake in a bag; exactly the failure you named.

steps.path: The host chip on a chat
steps.headline: You tap the chip to move a chat to a device that does not have its project. What should the chip do?
steps.today: No chip exists. Today's handoff refuses outright with a project-missing error.
steps.problem: A device without the project's files cannot host a project chat properly, but refusing silently is confusing.
steps.proposal: Pick how the chip treats such a device.

options.label: Fetch the project there, then switch
pros: Always works; the chip shows Preparing Desktop with progress, then the switch happens.
cons: A big project means a wait, and that device now holds the project.

options.label: Grey it out with the reason
pros: Nothing surprising happens.
cons: A dead end: you must fix it elsewhere first.

options.label: Allow it, with a warning
pros: Your choice, immediately.
cons: The assistant then answers about files it cannot see.

steps.headline: You asked for deliberate forking, like Claude Code has. When you open the original after forking it, what should happen?
steps.today: No fork feature exists in the app. Conflict copies are the only forks, and the app hides them.
steps.problem: An original and its fork share most of their text; opening the original by habit and continuing there creates two live versions again.
steps.proposal: Forks sit grouped under their original in the list. Pick what opening the original does.

options.label: Warn, offer to archive it
pros: Your words from the first deck: a notice that it was forked and continued elsewhere, with Archive original and resume from fork as one tap, or continue here anyway.
cons: One notice to read.

options.label: Archive the original automatically
pros: Nothing to read; the list stays clean.
cons: Removes a chat you may have forked precisely to keep both going.

options.label: Treat both as equals
pros: Simplest; both are just chats.
cons: Nothing stops you from continuing both and losing track of which has what.

steps.headline: Any rule I should check this design against that these two decks never asked about?
steps.today: Your first deck's answers plus this one cover scope, connection, what travels, the phone, sleep, switching and forks.
steps.problem: The next step is rewriting the design document from these answers. A rule I do not know cannot be written in.
steps.proposal: Write it in a line, or leave it empty.
steps.prompt: e.g. never ask me to install anything
